For $f : V \to \C$, $L, j \in \N$ and $x \in V$ the ball mean of differences of order $L$ at
level $j$ is
\[
  d_j f(x) = \frac{1}{|B_j|} \int_{B_j} |\Delta^L_h f(x)| \, dh \in [0, \infty] .
\]
For every $c > 0$ and $j \in \N$, $|B(0, c 2^{-j})| = c^n |B_j|$ (Mathlib's
\texttt{MeasureTheory.Measure.addHaar\_ball\_mul\_of\_pos}) and $2^{jn} |B_j| = |B(0,1)|$.
Let $1 \leq p < \infty$, $s \in \R$ and $1 \leq q \leq \infty$. For $f \in L_p$ the ball means
quasi-norm of Triebel--Lizorkin type is
\[
  \|f\|^{L}_{F^s_{p,q}, \Delta} = \|f\|_p + \Bigl\| x \mapsto \bigl\| (2^{js} d_j f(x))_{j \in \N}
  \bigr\|_{\ell_q} \Bigr\|_{L_p},
\]
and $x \mapsto \|(2^{js} d_j f(x))_j\|_{\ell_q}$ is measurable.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary properties of ball means]
\label{lem:ball-means-basic}
\lean{Rd.ballMeanDiff_le_of_forall, Rd.ballMeanDiff_level_add_le,
  Rd.measurable_enorm_higherDiff_step,
  Rd.measurable_ballMeanDiff, Rd.ballMeanDiff_congr_ae, Rd.ballMeanDiff_add_le,
  Rd.ballMeanDiff_zero, Rd.ballMeanDiff_finsetSum_le}
\leanok
\uses{def:ball-means-differences, lem:rd-differences}
For all $f, f' : V \to \C$, all $L, j, k \in \N$, every $x \in V$ and every $c \in [0, \infty]$:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item if $|\Delta^L_h f(x)| \leq c$ for every $h \in B_j$, then $d_j f(x) \leq c$;
  \item $d_{j+k} f(x) \leq 2^{kn} d_j f(x)$;
  \item if $f$ is measurable, then $h \mapsto |\Delta^L_h f(x)|$ and $d_j f$ are measurable;
  \item if $f = f'$ almost everywhere, then $d_j f = d_j f'$ almost everywhere;
  \item if $f$ is measurable, then $d_j(f + f')(x) \leq d_j f(x) + d_j f'(x)$, and
    $d_j \bigl(\sum_{i \in S} f_i\bigr)(x) \leq \sum_{i \in S} d_j f_i(x)$ for every finite
    family of measurable $f_i : V \to \C$; $d_j 0 = 0$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
(1) is the mean of a bounded function, and (2) holds since $B_{j+k} \subseteq B_j$ and
$|B_j| = 2^{kn} |B_{j+k}|$. (3) The function $(x, h) \mapsto |\Delta^L_h f(x)|$ is jointly
measurable (\Cref{lem:rd-differences}), and Tonelli's theorem gives the measurability of
$d_j f$. (4) At a point $x$ with
$f(x) = f'(x)$ the values $f(x + l h)$ and $f'(x + l h)$, $1 \leq l \leq L$, agree for almost
every $h$, since $h \mapsto x + l h$ maps null sets to null sets. (5) The triangle inequality
and the additivity of the integral, which needs one measurable summand; finite sums by
induction.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Ball means in $L_p$]
\label{lem:ball-means-lp}
\lean{Rd.ballMeanDiff_rpow_le, Rd.eLpNorm_ballMeanDiff_le_of_measurable,
  Rd.eLpNorm_ballMeanDiff_le}
\leanok
\uses{lem:ball-means-basic, lem:weighted-jensen, lem:rd-differences, lem:lp-norm-nonnegative}
For every measurable $f : V \to \C$, all $L, j \in \N$, every $P \geq 1$ and every $x \in V$,
$(d_j f(x))^P \leq |B_j|^{-1} \int_{B_j} |\Delta^L_h f(x)|^P \, dh$. For all $L, j \in \N$,
every $1 \leq p < \infty$ and every almost everywhere strongly measurable $f : V \to \C$,
$\|d_j f\|_p \leq 2^L \|f\|_p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The first bound is \Cref{lem:weighted-jensen} for the probability measure
$|B_j|^{-1} \mathbf 1_{B_j}(h) \, dh$. Integrating over $x$ and exchanging the integrals,
$\int (d_j f)^p \leq |B_j|^{-1} \int_{B_j} \|\Delta^L_h f\|_p^p \, dh \leq (2^L \|f\|_p)^p$ by
\Cref{lem:rd-differences}. A general $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a measurable function, and
\Cref{lem:ball-means-basic} (4) transfers the bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Local means by ball means]
\label{thm:local-means-by-ball-means}
\lean{Rd.LocalMeansBump.iSup_enorm_lt_top, Rd.LocalMeansBump.ballMeanConst,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.ballMeanConst_ne_top, Rd.ofReal_abs_inv_neg_inv_two_pow_pow,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.smul_closedBall_subset_ball,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.lintegral_enorm_mul_higherDiff_le,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_localMean_le_ballMeanDiff}
\leanok
\uses{def:local-means, def:ball-means-differences, lem:conv-second-argument, lem:conv-assoc,
  lem:schwartz-tails}
Let
\[
  C^\Delta = \sup |g| \, |B(0,1)| \, 2^{rn} (1 + 2^n);
\]
then $C^\Delta < \infty$. For every $L \in \N$, every $1 \leq p < \infty$, every $f \in L_p$,
almost every $x \in V$ and every $j \in \N$,
\[
  |(k_{j+r+1} * f)(x)| \leq C^\Delta \, d_j f(x) .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Let $J = j + r$. Since $k_{J+1} = m_{2^{J+1}} - m_{2^J}$,
$k_{J+1} * f = (f - m_{2^J} * f) - (f - m_{2^{J+1}} * f)$ almost everywhere, and by
\Cref{lem:conv-second-argument}, for $c = 2^{J}$ and $c = 2^{J+1}$,
$|f(x) - (m_c * f)(x)| \leq \int |g(z)| \, |\Delta^L_{-z/c} f(x)| \, dz$ almost everywhere. The
bump vanishes outside $\bar B(0, R)$, and the substitution $h = -z/c$
(\Cref{lem:schwartz-tails}) gives at most $\sup |g| \, c^n \int_{\bar B(0, R/c)}
|\Delta^L_h f(x)| \, dh$. Since $R < 2^r$, $\bar B(0, R/c) \subseteq B_j$, and
$c^n |B_j|$ is $2^{rn} |B(0,1)|$ for $c = 2^J$ and $2^{(r+1)n} |B(0,1)|$ for $c = 2^{J+1}$. The
sum of the two bounds is $C^\Delta d_j f(x)$.
\end{proof}

Young's inequality bounds the first $r + 1$ local means by $\|f\|_p$
(\Cref{thm:tl-ball-means}).

\begin{lemma}[Tools for ball means of convolutions]
\label{lem:moving-balls}
\lean{Rd.enorm_le_inv_two_pow_of_mem_ball, Rd.dyadicWeight_mul_dyadicWeight_neg_of_le,
  Rd.volume_setOf_dist_add_smul_lt_le, Rd.indicator_ball_add_smul_le,
  Rd.setLIntegral_indicator_ball_add_smul_le, Rd.setLIntegral_setLIntegral_ball_le}
\leanok
\uses{def:ball-means-differences}
For every $j \in \N$, every $h \in B_j$ has $|h| \leq 2^{-j}$. For all $i, j \in \N$ with
$i \leq j$ and every $L \in \R$, $2^{iL} 2^{-jL} = 2^{-(j-i)L}$. For every real $l \geq 1$, all
$a, \rho \in \R$, all $x, w \in V$ and every $G : V \to [0, \infty]$,
$|\{v : |x + l v - w| < \rho\}| \leq |B(0, \rho)|$ and
\[
  \int_{B(0,a)} 1_{B(x + l v, \rho)}(w) \, G(w) \, dv \leq |B(0, \rho)| \,
  1_{B(x, \rho + l a)}(w) \, G(w) ;
\]
if $G$ is almost everywhere measurable, then
\[
  \int_{B(0,a)} \int_{B(x + l v, \rho)} G(w) \, dw \, dv \leq |B(0, \rho)|
  \int_{B(x, \rho + l a)} G .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The set $\{v : |x + l v - w| < \rho\}$ is the ball $B((w - x)/l, \rho/l)$, of measure
$l^{-n} |B(0,\rho)|$. A point $w$ of $B(x + l v, \rho)$ with $|v| < a$ satisfies
$|w - x| < \rho + l a$ by the triangle inequality, and $v$ lies in this set, which gives the
single integral. For the double integral, exchange the integrals and apply the single integral at
every $w$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Ball means of the dual kernels]
\label{thm:ball-means-dual}
\lean{Rd.LocalMeansBump.diffByLocalMeansConst, Rd.LocalMeansBump.diffByLocalMeansConst_ne_top,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_higherDiff_dual_le_mul,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_higherDiff_dual_le_indicator,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_higherDiff_conv_dual_le_of_le,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.ballMeanDiff_conv_dual_le_of_le, Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_dual_le_indicator,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_conv_dual_le, Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_conv_dual_le_maximal,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.laverage_enorm_conv_dual_add_smul_le_of_one_le,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.laverage_enorm_conv_dual_add_smul_le,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.ballMeanDiff_conv_dual_le_of_lt, Rd.LocalMeansBump.ballMeanDiff_conv_dual_le}
\leanok
\uses{lem:dual-kernel-derivatives, lem:dual-kernel-bounds, lem:dual-averaged-differences,
  lem:smooth-differences, lem:conv-pointwise, lem:moving-balls, lem:maximal-function-kernels,
  def:maximal-function, lem:ball-means-basic}
Let $L \in \N$ and
\[
  E_L = |B(0,1)| \max\bigl( A_{L,L} (2LR + L + 1)^n, \;
  2^L A_{L,0} (2LR + 1)^n (2LR + L + 1)^n \bigr);
\]
then $E_L < \infty$. For every locally integrable $u : V \to \C$, all $i, j \in \N$ and every
$x \in V$,
\[
  d_j(\eta_i * u)(x) \leq E_L \, c^L_{ji} \, M|u|(x) .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Case $i \leq j$. For $h \in B_j$, $\Delta^L_h (\eta_i * u) = (\Delta^L_h \eta_i) * u$
(\Cref{lem:conv-pointwise}), and by \Cref{lem:smooth-differences} and
\Cref{lem:dual-kernel-derivatives},
$|\Delta^L_h \eta_i| \leq A_{L,L} 2^{in} 2^{iL} |h|^L \leq A_{L,L} 2^{in} 2^{-(j-i)L}$;
the difference vanishes outside $B(0, (2LR + L + 1) 2^{-i})$
(\Cref{lem:dual-averaged-differences}). \Cref{lem:maximal-function-kernels} (1) bounds
$|\Delta^L_h (\eta_i * u)(x)|$ by $A_{L,L} (2LR + L + 1)^n |B(0,1)| 2^{-(j-i)L} M|u|(x)$ for
every $h$, hence also the mean $d_j(\eta_i * u)(x)$.

Case $i > j$. By \Cref{lem:conv-pointwise},
$|\Delta^L_h (\eta_i * u)(x)| \leq \sum_{l \leq L} \binom{L}{l} |(\eta_i * u)(x + l h)|$, and
$|\eta_i| \leq A_{L,0} 2^{in} \mathbf 1_{B(0, \rho_i)}$ with $\rho_i = (2LR + 1) 2^{-i}$
(\Cref{lem:dual-kernel-bounds}), so
$|(\eta_i * u)(v)| \leq A_{L,0} 2^{in} \int_{B(v, \rho_i)} |u|$ for every $v \in V$
(\Cref{lem:maximal-function-kernels} (1)). For $l = 0$ this is at most
$A_{L,0} (2LR + 1)^n |B(0,1)| M|u|(x)$. For $l \geq 1$ the mean over $h \in B_j$ is at most
$|B_j|^{-1} A_{L,0} 2^{in} |B(0, \rho_i)| \int_{B(x, (2LR + L + 1) 2^{-j})} |u|$ by
\Cref{lem:moving-balls}, since $\rho_i + l 2^{-j} \leq (2LR + L + 1) 2^{-j}$, and this is at most
$A_{L,0} (2LR + 1)^n (2LR + L + 1)^n |B(0,1)| M|u|(x)$. The binomial weights sum to $2^L$.
\end{proof}

For a single step $h$ the ball $B(x + l h, \rho_i)$ lies in $B(x, (2LR + L + 1) 2^{-j})$, which
costs the factor $2^{(i-j)n}$; the average over the steps $h \in B_j$ removes it.

\begin{theorem}[Ball means by local means]
\label{thm:ball-means-by-local-means}
\lean{Rd.LocalMeansBump.ballMeanDiff_partialSum_le, Rd.LocalMeansBump.ballMeanDiff_le_tsum_add,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.tendsto_eLpNorm_ballMeanDiff_sub,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.ballMeanDiff_le_tsum_maximal}
\leanok
\uses{thm:ball-means-dual, lem:reproducing-formula, lem:reproducing-pointwise,
  lem:ball-means-basic, lem:ball-means-lp, lem:limits-of-pointwise-bounds,
  lem:maximal-function-basic, lem:maximal-function-measurable, def:tl-local-means, lem:conv-op}
Let $L \in \N$ with $L \geq 1$ and $1 \leq p < \infty$. For every $f \in L_p$, almost every
$x \in V$ and every $j \in \N$,
\[
  d_j f(x) \leq E_L \sum_{i \in \N} c^L_{ji} \, M|k_i * f|(x) .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Let $F_J = m_{2^J} * m_{2^J} * f = \sum_{i \leq J} \eta_i * (k_i * f)$, an identity of continuous
functions (\Cref{lem:reproducing-pointwise}). By \Cref{lem:ball-means-basic} (5) and
\Cref{thm:ball-means-dual}, with $M|k_i * f|$ unchanged when $k_i * f$ changes on a null set,
$d_j F_J(x) \leq E_L \sum_{i \leq J} c^L_{ji} M|k_i * f|(x)$ for every $x$, and
$d_j f \leq d_j F_J + d_j(f - F_J)$ everywhere. Since $F_J \to f$ in $L_p$
(\Cref{lem:reproducing-formula}), $\|d_j(f - F_J)\|_p \leq 2^L \|f - F_J\|_p \to 0$
(\Cref{lem:ball-means-lp}), and \Cref{lem:limits-of-pointwise-bounds} gives the bound almost
everywhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Ball means characterisation of Triebel--Lizorkin spaces]
\label{thm:tl-ball-means}
\lean{Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_le_tlLocalMeansNorm, Rd.LocalMeansBump.diffUpperConst,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.diffUpperConst_ne_top, Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlDiffNorm_le_tlLocalMeansNorm,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.diffLowerConst, Rd.LocalMeansBump.diffLowerConst_ne_top,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.eLpNorm_dyadicWeight_mul_conv_kernel_le,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.lqNorm_localMean_shift_le, Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlLocalMeansNorm_le_tlDiffNorm}
\leanok
\uses{thm:ball-means-by-local-means, thm:local-means-by-ball-means,
  lem:almost-diagonal-pointwise, lem:maximal-bounds-mixed-norm, lem:reproducing-formula,
  lem:dual-kernel-moduli, lem:conv-op, cor:mixed-norm-sandwich, lem:lq-basic,
  thm:rd-atomic-synthesis, def:tl-local-means, def:ball-means-differences,
  lem:lp-norm-nonnegative}
Let $s \in \R$, $L \in \N$, $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $1 \leq q \leq \infty$, and let
\[
  D^\Delta_{L,s} = 2 \|m\|_1 \sum_{j \leq r} 2^{js} + 2^{(r+1)s} C^\Delta .
\]
Then $D^\Delta_{L,s} < \infty$, and for every $f \in L_p$,
\[
  \|f\|^{g,L}_{F^s_{p,q}} \leq D^\Delta_{L,s} \, \|f\|^{L}_{F^s_{p,q}, \Delta} .
\]
If $L \geq 1$, then $\|f\|_p \leq 2 \|m\|_1 (1 - 2^{-s})^{-1} \|f\|^{g,L}_{F^s_{p,q}}$ for every
$f \in L_p$. If $L \geq 1$, $1 < p$ and $1 < q$, let
\[
  U^\Delta_{L,p,q,s} = 2 \|m\|_1 (1 - 2^{-s})^{-1} + E_L A_{s,L} C_{n,p,q},
\]
with the constants $A_{s,L}$ of \Cref{lem:almost-diagonal-pointwise} and $C_{n,p,q}$ of
\Cref{thm:fefferman-stein}; then $U^\Delta_{L,p,q,s} < \infty$ for $0 < s < L$, and for every
$f \in L_p$,
\[
  \|f\|^{L}_{F^s_{p,q}, \Delta} \leq U^\Delta_{L,p,q,s} \, \|f\|^{g,L}_{F^s_{p,q}} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Lower bound: pointwise
$\|(2^{js} |k_j * f(x)|)_j\|_{\ell_q} \leq \sum_{j \leq r} 2^{js} |k_j * f(x)| +
\|(2^{(j+r+1)s} |k_{j+r+1} * f(x)|)_j\|_{\ell_q}$ (\Cref{lem:lq-basic}); the head is bounded by
Young's inequality $\|k_j * f\|_p \leq 2 \|m\|_1 \|f\|_p$ (\Cref{lem:conv-op},
\Cref{lem:dual-kernel-moduli}), the tail by \Cref{thm:local-means-by-ball-means}, almost
everywhere, after $2^{(j+r+1)s} = 2^{(r+1)s} 2^{js}$.

Upper bound: the reproducing formula $f = \sum_j \eta_j * k_j * f$ (\Cref{lem:reproducing-formula})
with $\|\eta_j\|_1 \leq 2 \|m\|_1$ gives
$\|f\|_p \leq 2 \|m\|_1 (1 - 2^{-s})^{-1} \sup_j 2^{js} \|k_j * f\|_p$ (the series bound of
\Cref{thm:rd-atomic-synthesis}), and $\sup_j 2^{js} \|k_j * f\|_p \leq \|f\|^{g,L}_{F^s_{p,q}}$
by \Cref{cor:mixed-norm-sandwich} at $q = \infty$ and $\ell_q \subseteq \ell_\infty$.
\Cref{thm:ball-means-by-local-means} and \Cref{lem:almost-diagonal-pointwise} bound
$\|(2^{js} d_j f(x))_j\|_{\ell_q}$ by $E_L A_{s,L} \|(M(2^{is} |k_i * f|)(x))_i\|_{\ell_q}$
almost everywhere, and \Cref{lem:maximal-bounds-mixed-norm} finishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Ball means describe $\TL{s}{p}{q}$]
\label{cor:tl-ball-means}
\lean{Rd.memTriebelLizorkin_iff_tlDiffNorm_lt_top}
\leanok
\uses{thm:tl-ball-means, thm:tl-local-means, thm:smooth-atomic-decomposition}
For every $1 < p < \infty$, every $1 < q \leq \infty$, every $L \in \N$, every $0 < s < L$ and
every $f \in L_p$, $f \in \TL{s}{p}{q}$ if and only if $\|f\|^{L}_{F^s_{p,q}, \Delta} < \infty$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$L \geq 1$ since $0 < s < L$. Both conditions are equivalent to the finiteness of the local means
quasi-norm of the standard bump (\Cref{thm:smooth-atomic-decomposition}), by
\Cref{thm:tl-local-means} and \Cref{thm:tl-ball-means}.
\end{proof}

\section{The atomic characterisation}

This section describes $\TL{s}{p}{q}$ by atomic decompositions, in the range $1 < p < \infty$,
$1 < q \leq \infty$, $0 < s < L$. As in the previous sections, $g$ is a bump of radius $R$,
$m^g$ its moment kernel of order $L$, $A_L = 2 \sup_V |m^g|$ the constant of
\Cref{lem:local-means-kernel-bounds}, $k_j$ and $\eta_j$ are the local means kernels and the dual
kernels, and $c^L_{ij} = 2^{-(i-j)L}$ for $j \leq i$, $c^L_{ij} = 1$ for $j > i$. The cells
$P_{j,m}$ and their centres $c_{j,m}$ are those of \Cref{def:dyadic-cells}, $|B_1|$ is the
volume of the unit ball, and $A_+ = \max(A, 0)$ for $A \in \R$. The atoms are the smooth atoms
of \Cref{def:smooth-atoms}, normalised in $L_\infty$; their constants are nonnegative
(\Cref{lem:smooth-atoms-basic}), so $A_+ = A$ for them. The coefficient of a cell in the
decomposition of $F$ is the mean of $|k_j * F|$ over the cell, at most a multiple of
$M(k_j * F)$ at every point of the cell. The Besov spaces use atoms normalised in $L_p$
(\Cref{thm:atomic-characterisation}); here the maximal function bounds means in $L_1$, so the
coefficients are $L_1$ means over the cells. Triebel~\cite{TriebelII} uses $(s,p)$-atoms
normalised in $L_p$; his coefficients are $2^{j(s - n/p)} \lambda_{j,m}$ for the coefficients
$\lambda_{j,m}$ here.

\begin{definition}[The sequence space $f^s_{p,q}$]
\label{def:tl-sequence-space}
\lean{Rd.cellCoefFun, Rd.cellCoefFun_of_mem, Rd.measurable_cellCoefFun, Rd.tlCoeffNorm,
  Rd.aemeasurable_lqNorm_cellCoefFun}
\leanok
\uses{def:dyadic-cells, def:lq-norm, lem:lp-norm-nonnegative}
Let $\lambda = (\lambda_{j,m})_{j \in \N, m \in \Z^n}$ be complex coefficients. For $j \in \N$ and
$x \in V$ let $\lambda_j(x) = |\lambda_{j,m}|$ for the index $m$ of the cell $P_{j,m}$ of level
$j$ that contains $x$. The function $\lambda_j : V \to [0, \infty)$ is measurable. For
$1 \leq p < \infty$, $s \in \R$ and $1 \leq q \leq \infty$,
\[
  \|\lambda\|_{f^s_{p,q}} = \Bigl\| x \mapsto \bigl\| (2^{js} \lambda_j(x))_{j \in \N}
  \bigr\|_{\ell_q} \Bigr\|_{L_p} ,
\]
and $x \mapsto \|(2^{js} \lambda_j(x))_j\|_{\ell_q}$ is measurable.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Coefficients and the maximal function]
\label{lem:coefficients-maximal}
\lean{Rd.volume_ball_div_two_pow, Rd.dyadicWeight_mul_setLIntegral_ball_le,
  Rd.cellCoefFun_le_maximal, Rd.enorm_coef_le_maximal_cellCoefFun,
  Rd.dyadicWeight_mul_tsum_ite_le_maximal, ENNReal.tsum_mul_le_of_le}
\leanok
\uses{def:tl-sequence-space, def:maximal-function, lem:dyadic-cubes, lem:dyadic-cells,
  lem:cells-partition, lem:product-modulus}
Let $\lambda$ be complex coefficients and $j \in \N$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item For every $m \in \Z^n$, $|P_{j,m}| = 2^{-jn}$; for every $\rho > 0$ and every $z \in V$,
    $|B(z, \rho 2^{-j})| = \rho^n |B_1| 2^{-jn}$, and for every $u : V \to [0, \infty]$ and every
    $x \in V$, $2^{jn} \int_{B(x, \rho 2^{-j})} u \leq \rho^n |B_1| \, M u(x)$.
  \item For every $u : V \to [0, \infty]$ with $|\lambda_{j,m}| \leq 2^{jn} \int_{P_{j,m}} u$
    for every $m \in \Z^n$, and every $x \in V$,
    $\lambda_j(x) \leq (2n + 1)^n |B_1| \, M u(x)$.
  \item For every $\rho \in \R$, every $m \in \Z^n$ and every $x \in V$ with
    $\|x - c_{j,m}\| \leq \rho 2^{-j}$, $|\lambda_{j,m}| \leq (2(\rho + 1))^n M \lambda_j(x)$.
  \item For every $i \leq j$, every $\rho \geq 0$ and every $x \in V$,
    \[
      2^{-jn} \sum_{m : \|x - c_{j,m}\| \leq \rho 2^{-i}} |\lambda_{j,m}| \leq
      (\rho + n + 1)^n |B_1| \, 2^{-in} M \lambda_j(x) .
    \]
  \item For every family $(\mu_m)$ in $[0, \infty]$, every predicate $P$ on the indices, every
    $B \in [0, \infty]$ and all $u_m \in [0, \infty]$ with $u_m \leq B \, \mathbf 1_{P(m)}$,
    $\sum_m \mu_m u_m \leq B \sum_{m : P(m)} \mu_m$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
(1) The cell is a cube of side $2^{-j}$ (\Cref{lem:dyadic-cubes}), the volume of balls scales
with the $n$-th power of the radius, $(2^{-j})^n = 2^{-jn}$ (\Cref{lem:product-modulus}), and
\Cref{def:maximal-function}. (2) The cell of $x$ lies in
$B(x, (2n + 1) 2^{-j})$, since all its points have distance at most $n 2^{-j}$ from its centre
(\Cref{lem:dyadic-cells}); apply (1). (3) $\rho \geq 0$ since $\|x - c_{j,m}\| \geq 0$. The ball
$B(c_{j,m}, 2^{-j}/2)$ lies in $P_{j,m}$
(\Cref{lem:dyadic-cubes}), where $\lambda_j = |\lambda_{j,m}|$, and in
$B(x, (\rho + 1) 2^{-j})$, whose volume is $(2(\rho + 1))^n$ times as large. (4) The cells in the
sum lie in $B(x, (\rho + n + 1) 2^{-i})$, and $2^{-jn} |\lambda_{j,m}| = \int_{P_{j,m}} \lambda_j$;
the cells are disjoint (\Cref{lem:cells-partition}), and (1) at level $i$ finishes. (5) is
termwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Smooth atoms on $V$]
\label{lem:smooth-atoms-basic}
\lean{Rd.IsSmoothAtom.norm_le, Rd.IsSmoothAtom.const_nonneg, Rd.IsSmoothAtom.continuous,
  Rd.IsSmoothAtom.hasCompactSupport, Rd.IsSmoothAtom.integrable,
  Rd.IsSmoothAtom.lintegral_enorm_le}
\leanok
\uses{def:smooth-atoms, lem:pointwise-atoms}
Let $a$ be a smooth atom on a set $\Omega$ of level $j$ with centre $c$, radius factor $d$ and
constant $A$. Then $|a| \leq A$ on $\Omega$, and $a$ has compact support. If $\Omega = V$, then
$A \geq 0$, $a$ is continuous and integrable, and for $d \geq 0$,
$\int_V |a| \leq A \, d^n |B_1| \, 2^{-jn}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The bound is the case $l = 0$ of \Cref{def:smooth-atoms}; for $\Omega = V$ it gives
$0 \leq |a(0)| \leq A$. The atom vanishes outside $\overline B(c, d 2^{-j})$, whose volume is
$d^n |B_1| 2^{-jn}$ (\Cref{lem:pointwise-atoms}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Convolution with a series of atoms]
\label{lem:conv-atom-series}
\lean{Rd.conv_tsum_atom, Rd.enorm_conv_le_tsum_atom}
\leanok
\uses{lem:smooth-atoms-basic, lem:cells-partition, lem:bounded-overlap, lem:cell-decomposition,
  def:conv}
Let $K$ be continuous with $K = 0$ outside $\overline B(0, \rho)$, $\rho \geq 0$, let $d \geq 0$,
and for every $m \in \Z^n$ let $a_m$ be a smooth atom on $V$ of level $j$ with centre $c_{j,m}$,
radius factor $d$ and constant $A$. For all complex $\lambda_m$ and every $x \in V$,
\[
  \Bigl(K * \sum_m \lambda_m a_m\Bigr)(x) = \sum_m \lambda_m (K * a_m)(x) ,
\]
and for every $f : V \to \C$ with $f = \sum_m \lambda_m a_m$ almost everywhere,
$|(K * f)(x)| \leq \sum_m |\lambda_m| \, |(K * a_m)(x)|$ for every $x \in V$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
If $K(y) \neq 0$ and $a_m(x - y) \neq 0$, then $\|x - c_{j,m}\| \leq \rho + d 2^{-j}$; only
finitely many centres satisfy this (\Cref{lem:cells-partition}, \Cref{lem:bounded-overlap}), so
\Cref{lem:cell-decomposition} (3) applies to $u_m = \lambda_m a_m$. The bound follows since
$K * f = K * \sum_m \lambda_m a_m$ (\Cref{def:conv}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Coarse local means of atoms]
\label{lem:coarse-local-means-atoms}
\lean{Rd.LocalMeansBump.lintegral_enorm_kernel_mul_atom_le,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlAtomCoarseConst, Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlAtomCoarseConst_ne_top,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_conv_kernel_level_le_of_le}
\leanok
\uses{lem:local-means-kernel-bounds, lem:reproducing-pointwise, lem:dyadic-weights-integer,
  lem:smooth-atoms-basic, lem:conv-atom-series, lem:coefficients-maximal, lem:weighted-jensen}
Let $L \in \N$, $d \geq 0$ and $A \in \R$, and let
\[
  C^{\mathrm c}_{L,d,A} = A_L \, A_+ \, d^n |B_1| \, (2LR + d + n + 1)^n |B_1| ;
\]
then $C^{\mathrm c}_{L,d,A} < \infty$. For all $i \leq j$, every smooth atom $a$ on $V$ of level
$j$ with centre $c$, radius factor $d$ and constant $A$, and every $x \in V$,
\[
  \int_V |k_i(y)| \, |a(x - y)| \, dy \leq A_L \, A_+ \, d^n |B_1| \, 2^{in} 2^{-jn}
  \mathbf 1_{\|x - c\| \leq (2LR + d) 2^{-i}} .
\]
For all $i \leq j$, all coefficients $\lambda$, smooth atoms $a_{j,m}$ on $V$ of level $j$ with
centres $c_{j,m}$, radius factor $d$ and constant $A$, every $f : V \to \C$ with
$f = \sum_m \lambda_{j,m} a_{j,m}$ almost everywhere and every $x \in V$,
\[
  |(k_i * f)(x)| \leq C^{\mathrm c}_{L,d,A} \, M \lambda_j(x) .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The kernel $k_i$ is continuous (\Cref{lem:reproducing-pointwise}), and
$|k_i| \leq A_L 2^{in}$ vanishes outside $\overline B(0, 2LR 2^{-i})$
(\Cref{lem:local-means-kernel-bounds}, \Cref{lem:dyadic-weights-integer}). Moreover
$\int |a| \leq A d^n |B_1| 2^{-jn}$ with $A = A_+$ (\Cref{lem:smooth-atoms-basic}); if
$\|x - c\| > (2LR + d) 2^{-i}$, then $\|x - y - c\| > d 2^{-i} \geq d 2^{-j}$ wherever
$k_i(y) \neq 0$. By \Cref{lem:conv-atom-series} and \Cref{lem:weighted-jensen},
$|(k_i * f)(x)| \leq A_L A_+ d^n |B_1| 2^{in} \cdot 2^{-jn}
\sum_{m : \|x - c_{j,m}\| \leq (2LR + d) 2^{-i}} |\lambda_{j,m}|$, and
\Cref{lem:coefficients-maximal} (4) bounds the last factor by
$(2LR + d + n + 1)^n |B_1| 2^{-in} M \lambda_j(x)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Fine local means of atoms]
\label{lem:fine-local-means-atoms}
\lean{Rd.IsSmoothAtom.higherDiff_eq_zero_of_lt, Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_mul_higherDiff_atom_le,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.ae_enorm_atom_sub_conv_scaled_le, Rd.LocalMeansBump.momentAtomConst,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.momentAtomConst_ne_top,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.ae_enorm_conv_kernel_atom_le_of_lt, Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlAtomFineConst,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlAtomFineConst_ne_top,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.ae_enorm_conv_kernel_level_le_of_lt}
\leanok
\uses{lem:smooth-atoms-regular, lem:local-means-one-scale, lem:conv-second-argument,
  def:local-means, lem:local-means-kernel-bounds, lem:reproducing-pointwise, def:rd-modulus,
  def:rd-modulus-on, lem:smooth-atoms-basic, lem:conv-atom-series, lem:coefficients-maximal}
Let $L \in \N$ with $L \geq 1$, $d \geq 0$ and $A \in \R$, and let
\[
  D_{L,A} = 2 \|g\|_1 \, 2^L L^{L+1} A_+ \, (2R)^L , \qquad
  C^{\mathrm f}_{L,d,A} = D_{L,A} \, (d + LR + n + 1)^n |B_1| ;
\]
then both are finite. For all $j < i$ and every smooth atom $a$ on $V$ of level $j$ and order
$L$ with centre $c$, radius factor $d$ and constant $A$, almost everywhere
\[
  |(k_i * a)(x)| \leq D_{L,A} \, 2^{-(i-j)L} \, \mathbf 1_{\|x - c\| \leq (d + LR) 2^{-j}} .
\]
For all $j < i$, all coefficients $\lambda$, smooth atoms $a_{j,m}$ on $V$ of level $j$ and order
$L$ with centres $c_{j,m}$, radius factor $d$ and constant $A$, and every $f : V \to \C$ with
$f = \sum_m \lambda_{j,m} a_{j,m}$ almost everywhere, almost everywhere
\[
  |(k_i * f)(x)| \leq C^{\mathrm f}_{L,d,A} \, 2^{-(i-j)L} \, M \lambda_j(x) .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
By \Cref{lem:local-means-one-scale} it suffices to show, for every $k \geq j$ and almost every
$x$,
\[
  |a(x) - (m^g_{2^k} * a)(x)| \leq \|g\|_1 \, 2^L L^{L+1} A_+ R^L \, 2^{-(k-j)L}
  \mathbf 1_{\|x - c\| \leq (d + LR) 2^{-j}} ,
\]
since $2 \cdot 2^L$ times this constant is $D_{L,A}$. By \Cref{lem:conv-second-argument},
$|a(x) - (m^g_{2^k} * a)(x)| \leq \int |g(z)| \, |\Delta^L_{-2^{-k} z} a(x)| \, dz$ almost
everywhere. On the support of $g$ the step $h = -2^{-k} z$ has $\|h\| \leq R 2^{-k}$, so
$|\Delta^L_h a(x)| \leq 2^L L^{L+1} A (2^j \|h\|)^L \leq 2^L L^{L+1} A R^L 2^{-(k-j)L}$
(\Cref{lem:smooth-atoms-regular}, with the steps of \Cref{def:rd-modulus-on}). The difference
is a sum of values $a(x + l h)$, $l \leq L$ (\Cref{def:rd-modulus}), which vanish when
$\|x - c\| > d 2^{-j} + L \|h\|$; since $\|h\| \leq R 2^{-j}$, they vanish unless
$\|x - c\| \leq (d + LR) 2^{-j}$. For the level, \Cref{lem:conv-atom-series} and
\Cref{lem:coefficients-maximal} (5) give
$|(k_i * f)(x)| \leq D_{L,A} 2^{-(i-j)L} \sum_{m : \|x - c_{j,m}\| \leq (d + LR) 2^{-j}}
|\lambda_{j,m}|$, and \Cref{lem:coefficients-maximal} (4) with $i = j$ bounds the sum by
$(d + LR + n + 1)^n |B_1| M \lambda_j(x)$.
\end{proof}

The fine local means need no moment conditions on the atoms: the moments of the kernel $k_i$ and
the smoothness of the atoms give the decay $2^{-(i-j)L}$.

\begin{theorem}[Synthesis from atoms]
\label{thm:tl-atomic-synthesis}
\lean{Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlAtomSynthesisConst, Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlAtomSynthesisConst_ne_top,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.ae_enorm_conv_kernel_level_le,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_conv_kernel_le_tsum_level,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.enorm_localMean_le_tsum_maximal_cellCoefFun,
  Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlLocalMeansNorm_le_tlCoeffNorm}
\leanok
\uses{lem:coarse-local-means-atoms, lem:fine-local-means-atoms, lem:lp-limits-pointwise,
  def:tl-local-means, lem:conv-op, lem:almost-diagonal-pointwise, lem:maximal-bounds-mixed-norm,
  def:tl-sequence-space}
Let $L \in \N$ with $L \geq 1$, $d \geq 0$, $A \in \R$, and
$C^{\mathrm a}_{L,d,A} = \max(C^{\mathrm c}_{L,d,A}, C^{\mathrm f}_{L,d,A}) < \infty$. Let
$1 < p < \infty$, $1 < q \leq \infty$ and $s \in \R$. For all coefficients $\lambda$, all smooth
atoms $a_{j,m}$ on $V$ of level $j$ and order $L$ with centres $c_{j,m}$, radius factor $d$ and
constant $A$, all $f_j \in L_p$ with $f_j = \sum_m \lambda_{j,m} a_{j,m}$ almost everywhere, and
every $F \in L_p$ with $\sum_{j \leq J} f_j \to F$ in $L_p$, almost everywhere and for all
$i \in \N$
\[
  |(k_i * F)(x)| \leq C^{\mathrm a}_{L,d,A} \sum_{j \in \N} c^L_{ij} \, M \lambda_j(x) ,
\]
and
\[
  \|F\|^{g,L}_{F^s_{p,q}} \leq C^{\mathrm a}_{L,d,A} \, A_{s,L} \, C_{n,p,q} \,
  \|\lambda\|_{f^s_{p,q}} ,
\]
with the constants $A_{s,L}$ of \Cref{lem:almost-diagonal-pointwise}, finite for $0 < s < L$,
and $C_{n,p,q}$ of \Cref{thm:fefferman-stein}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\Cref{lem:coarse-local-means-atoms} for $j \geq i$ and \Cref{lem:fine-local-means-atoms} for
$j < i$ give $|(k_i * f_j)(x)| \leq C^{\mathrm a}_{L,d,A} c^L_{ij} M \lambda_j(x)$ almost
everywhere. The local mean $k_i *$ is continuous on $L_p$ (\Cref{lem:conv-op}), so
$k_i * \sum_{j \leq J} f_j \to k_i * F$, and the bound
$|k_i * \sum_{j \leq J} f_j| \leq \sum_j |k_i * f_j|$ of the partial sums passes to $F$
(\Cref{lem:lp-limits-pointwise}). \Cref{lem:almost-diagonal-pointwise} with the local means index
$i$ and the level $j$ and \Cref{lem:maximal-bounds-mixed-norm} for the functions
$2^{js} \lambda_j$ finish.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Coefficients with exponent one]
\label{lem:cell-coefficients-exponent-one}
\lean{Rd.enorm_cellCoef_one_le, Rd.lqNorm_cellCoefFun_le_lqNorm_maximal}
\leanok
\uses{def:cell-atoms, lem:coefficients-maximal, lem:almost-diagonal-pointwise, lem:lq-basic}
For every almost everywhere strongly measurable $u : V \to \C$, every $j \in \N$ and every
$m \in \Z^n$, the coefficient $\lambda_{j,m}$ of $u$ with exponent $p = 1$
(\Cref{def:cell-atoms}) satisfies $|\lambda_{j,m}| \leq 2^{jn} \int_{P_{j,m}} |u|$. For all
almost everywhere strongly measurable $u_j : V \to \C$, $j \in \N$, the coefficients
$\lambda_{j,m}$ of $u_j$ with exponent one satisfy, for every $q$, every
$s \in \R$ and every $x \in V$,
\[
  \|(2^{js} \lambda_j(x))_j\|_{\ell_q} \leq (2n + 1)^n |B_1| \,
  \|(M(2^{js} |u_j|)(x))_j\|_{\ell_q} .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$\lambda_{j,m} = 2^{jn} \|1_{P_{j,m}} u\|_1$ when this is finite, and $0$ otherwise. The second
bound is \Cref{lem:coefficients-maximal} (2) for every level, with the weights moved inside the
maximal function (\Cref{lem:almost-diagonal-pointwise}).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Atomic decomposition of Triebel--Lizorkin type]
\label{thm:tl-atomic-decomposition}
\lean{Rd.LocalMeansBump.tl_atomic_decomposition, Rd.LocalMeansBump.tlCoeffNorm_cellCoef_le}
\leanok
\uses{lem:cell-atoms-smooth, lem:cell-decomposition, def:cell-atoms, lem:reproducing-formula,
  def:tl-local-means, lem:cell-coefficients-exponent-one, lem:maximal-bounds-mixed-norm,
  thm:young, def:local-means}
Let $L \in \N$ with $L \geq 1$, $K \in \N$, $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $F \in L_p$, and let
$u_j = k_j * F$. Then $u_j \in L_p$. For $j \in \N$ and $m \in \Z^n$ let
\[
  \lambda_{j,m} = 2^{jn} \int_{P_{j,m}} |u_j| , \qquad
  a_{j,m} = \lambda_{j,m}^{-1} \, \eta_j * (1_{P_{j,m}} u_j) ,
\]
with $a_{j,m} = 0$ if $\lambda_{j,m} = 0$: the coefficients and cell atoms with exponent $p = 1$
of \Cref{def:cell-atoms} for the kernel $\eta_j$ and $g = u_j$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item every $a_{j,m}$ is a smooth atom on $V$ of level $j$ and order $K$ with centre $c_{j,m}$,
    radius factor $2LR + n$ and constant $A_{L,K}$ of \Cref{lem:dual-kernel-derivatives};
  \item $(\eta_j * u_j)(x) = \sum_m \lambda_{j,m} a_{j,m}(x)$ for every $j \in \N$ and every
    $x \in V$;
  \item $\sum_{j \leq J} \eta_j * u_j \to F$ in $L_p$;
  \item if $p > 1$, then for every $1 < q \leq \infty$ and every $s \in \R$,
    \[
      \|\lambda\|_{f^s_{p,q}} \leq (2n + 1)^n |B_1| \, C_{n,p,q} \, \|F\|^{g,L}_{F^s_{p,q}} .
    \]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$u_j \in L_p$ by Young's inequality (\Cref{thm:young}), so $1_{P_{j,m}} u_j \in L_1$
(\Cref{lem:cell-decomposition}) and $\lambda_{j,m}$ is the finite integral. (1) is
\Cref{lem:cell-atoms-smooth} at $p = 1$, where the factor $((2LR)^n |B_1|)^{1 - 1/p}$ is $1$,
applied to $1_{P_{j,m}} u_j$; the atom of a cell depends only on $u_j$ on that cell
(\Cref{def:cell-atoms}). (2) is \Cref{lem:cell-decomposition} (4), and (3) is the reproducing
formula (\Cref{lem:reproducing-formula}). (4) is \Cref{lem:cell-coefficients-exponent-one} for
the continuous $u_j$ and \Cref{lem:maximal-bounds-mixed-norm} for the functions $2^{js} |u_j|$.
\end{proof}

The bound (4) uses neither $L \geq 1$ nor the order $K$.

\begin{corollary}[Atoms describe $\TL{s}{p}{q}$]
\label{cor:tl-atomic}
\lean{Rd.memTriebelLizorkin_iff_atomic}
\leanok
\uses{thm:tl-atomic-synthesis, thm:tl-atomic-decomposition, thm:tl-local-means,
  thm:smooth-atomic-decomposition}
For every $1 < p < \infty$, every $1 < q \leq \infty$, every $L \in \N$, every $0 < s < L$ and
every $F \in L_p$, $F \in \TL{s}{p}{q}$ if and only if there are $\rho \geq 0$, $A \in \R$,
complex coefficients $\lambda_{j,m}$, smooth atoms $a_{j,m}$ on $V$ of level $j$ and order $L$
with centres $c_{j,m}$, radius factor $\rho$ and constant $A$, and $f_j \in L_p$ with
$f_j = \sum_m \lambda_{j,m} a_{j,m}$ almost everywhere, $\sum_{j \leq J} f_j \to F$ in $L_p$ and
$\|\lambda\|_{f^s_{p,q}} < \infty$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$L \geq 1$ since $0 < s < L$, and $F \in \TL{s}{p}{q}$ iff the local means quasi-norm of a bump is
finite (\Cref{thm:tl-local-means}, with the bump of \Cref{thm:smooth-atomic-decomposition}).
Forward: \Cref{thm:tl-atomic-decomposition} with $K = L$, $\rho = 2LR + n$, $A = A_{L,L}$ and
$f_j = \eta_j * (k_j * F)$. Backward: \Cref{thm:tl-atomic-synthesis}, since
$A_{s,L} < \infty$.
\end{proof}

The Besov analogue is \Cref{thm:atomic-characterisation}. Here the atoms are indexed by the cells
and centred at their centres, which takes the place of the bounded overlap condition there, and
the atoms of the decomposition are smooth of every order.

\chapter{Sobolev spaces on $\R^d$}
\label{ch:sobolev-rd}

This chapter works on a finite-dimensional real inner product space $V$ of dimension $n$, such
as $\R^d$, with Lebesgue measure, and defines Sobolev spaces by weak derivatives. A weak
derivative is an identity between distributions on an open set $\Omega \subseteq V$, in Mathlib's
space $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ of distributions tested against real smooth compactly supported
functions. On the whole space $V$ and for $L_p$ functions it is the same as an identity between
tempered distributions, the setting of Mathlib's Fourier transform and Bessel potential spaces.
For $p = 2$, \Cref{sec:sobolev-two-littlewood-paley} identifies Mathlib's Bessel potential spaces
$H^s(V)$, $s \geq 0$, with the Triebel--Lizorkin spaces $\TL{s}{2}{2}$ (and, for $s > 0$, with the
Besov spaces $\Besov{s}{2}{2}$) and proves $\Sob{1}{2}(V) = H^1(V) = \Besov{1}{2}{2}$.
\Cref{sec:lipschitz-domain-h1} restricts $H^1(V)$ to bounded Lipschitz domains, describes the
restrictions by intrinsic differences, shows that they lie in $\Sob{1}{2}(\Omega)$, and
identifies their boundary traces with $B^{1/2}_{2,2}(\Gamma)$. \Cref{sec:rellich-compactness}
proves Rellich's theorem: the restriction from $H^1(V)$ to $L_2(\Omega)$ is compact for every
bounded $\Omega \subseteq V$. \Cref{sec:sobolev-restriction-spaces} builds the Hilbert spaces
$H^s(\Omega)$, $\tilde H^s(\Omega)$ and $H^s_0(\Omega)$ inside $H^s(V)$, for every open
$\Omega$ and every real $s$. \Cref{sec:sobolev-duality} proves the duality of
$\tilde H^s(\Omega)$ and $H^{-s}(\Omega)$. \Cref{sec:boundary-trace-space} builds the trace space
$H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ of a bounded Lipschitz domain, and \Cref{sec:lipschitz-graph-area} proves the
area formula for Lipschitz graphs, which expresses the Euclidean Hausdorff measure of the
boundary of a Lipschitz graph domain in its chart. \Cref{sec:surface-measure} builds the surface
measure $\mathcal H^{n-1}$ on the boundary of a bounded Lipschitz domain, $L_2(\Gamma)$ and the
traces into it.
\Cref{sec:dilation-families} starts the theory for $1 < p < \infty$: families of dilated
Schwartz kernels, their Fourier overlap and their H\"ormander condition.
\Cref{sec:convolution-adjoint} moves convolution kernels and their derivatives to the other side
of an integral and shows that weak derivatives commute with convolution by Schwartz functions.
\Cref{sec:plancherel-bounds} bounds the analysis and synthesis operators of a family of
integrable kernels on $L_2(V)$ by its Fourier overlap. \Cref{sec:calderon-zygmund-signed}
splits a function with values in a normed space, or a family of such functions, into a bounded
good part and bad pieces with mean zero on dyadic cubes. \Cref{sec:vector-valued-weak-type}
proves the weak type $(1,1)$ of the analysis and synthesis operators of every
Calder\'on--Zygmund family, with an explicit constant. \Cref{sec:weak-type-operators} takes over
the weak $L_p$ norms and the operators of weak and strong type of the formalisation of
Carleson's theorem, \Cref{sec:marcinkiewicz} proves Marcinkiewicz interpolation between weak
type $(1,1)$ and strong type $(2,2)$, and \Cref{sec:lp-norm-duality} computes $L_p$ norms by
duality. Together they give the strong type $(p,p)$, $1 < p < \infty$, of these operators in
\Cref{sec:vector-valued-strong-type}, and \Cref{sec:square-function} proves the square function
theorem $\TL{0}{p}{2} = L_p(V)$ with explicit constants. \Cref{sec:derivative-kernels} writes
the Littlewood--Paley blocks as sums of derivatives of Schwartz kernels, and
\Cref{sec:sobolev-triebel-lizorkin} proves $\Sob{m}{p}(V) = \TL{m}{p}{2}$ for
$1 < p < \infty$, with explicit constants and the Besov sandwich. \Cref{sec:sobolev-embedding}
proves the Nikolskii inequality for the blocks and from it the embeddings of Besov spaces into
$L_r(V)$ and into the bounded continuous functions, and the Sobolev embeddings
$\Sob{m}{p}(V) \hookrightarrow L_r(V)$ for $m > n(1/p - 1/r)$ and
$\Sob{m}{p}(V) \hookrightarrow C_b(V)$ for $m > n/p$, all with explicit constants.
\Cref{sec:bessel-kernels} prepares the Bessel potential spaces: the Bessel potential maps the
dilates of every Schwartz function to multiples of the dilates of its Bessel kernels; when the
Fourier transform of the function lives in an annulus, the Bessel kernels form a uniform Schwartz
family and their dilates a Calder\'on--Zygmund family.
\Cref{sec:bessel-potential-lifting} proves $\TL{s}{p}{2} \subseteq H^{s,p}(V)$ for every real
$s$ and $H^{s,p}(V) = \TL{s}{p}{2}$ for $s \geq 0$ and $1 < p < \infty$, hence Calder\'on's
theorem $\Sob{m}{p}(V) = H^{m,p}(V)$, with existential constants.
\Cref{sec:divergence-kernels} and \Cref{sec:sobolev-extension} prove the extension theorem for
$\Sob{1}{p}$ on bounded Lipschitz domains, $1 < p < \infty$. \Cref{sec:lipschitz-graph-green}
and \Cref{sec:lipschitz-domain-green} prove Gauss--Green on Lipschitz graph domains and Green's
formula on bounded Lipschitz domains, and \Cref{sec:trace-kernel} proves that the kernel of the
trace is $H^1_0(\Omega)$.

On a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega$, the space $H^1(\Omega)$ of this chapter
(\Cref{sec:lipschitz-domain-h1}) is the space of restrictions of $H^1(V)$, the definition of
Chandler-Wilde, Hewett and Moiola \cite{ChandlerWildeHewettMoiola}; for restrictions of $H^1(V)$,
Rellich's theorem holds on every bounded set (\Cref{sec:rellich-compactness}). Every restriction
lies in the space $\Sob{1}{2}(\Omega)$ of weak derivatives, on every open set. On bounded
Lipschitz domains the two spaces agree by the extension theorem of Calder\'on and Stein
\cite[Chapter VI]{SteinSingular} (\Cref{thm:sobolev-extension}); on some bounded
open sets $\Sob{1}{2}(\Omega)$ is strictly larger, as for a disc with a slit removed, and its
embedding into $L_2(\Omega)$ can fail to be compact, as for the rooms-and-passages domains
\cite[Chapter 6]{AdamsFournier}. The norm bounds of this chapter are explicit on $V$; on bounded
Lipschitz domains the extension and trace theorems carry existential constants, and the
statements are equivalences of membership. On bounded Lipschitz domains the functions of
$H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary trace zero form the closure of the test functions in $H^1(\Omega)$
\cite[Theorem 3.40]{McLean} (\Cref{thm:trace-kernel-zero-boundary}); the spaces $H^1(\Omega)$ and
$H^1_0(\Omega)$ of that theorem are the Hilbert spaces of \Cref{sec:sobolev-restriction-spaces}.

\section{Test functions in the Schwartz space}
\label{sec:schwartz-cutoff}

Throughout this chapter $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, for open $\Omega \subseteq V$, is the space of
smooth functions $\varphi : V \to \R$ with compact support in $\Omega$, and
$\mathcal S(V)$ is the space of complex Schwartz functions on $V$. For directions
$v = (v_0, \dots, v_{k-1}) \in V^k$ let $\partial^v = \partial_{v_0} \cdots \partial_{v_{k-1}}$ be
the iterated directional derivative, with $\partial^v = \mathrm{id}$ for $k = 0$. Mathlib
differentiates a distribution $T$ on $\Omega$ by $\partial_w T(\varphi) = T(-\partial_w \varphi)$
and a tempered distribution $T$ by $\partial_w T(u) = T(-\partial_w u)$. This section shows that
test functions are Schwartz functions with the same derivatives, and that they determine
tempered distributions.

\begin{definition}[Test functions as Schwartz functions]
\label{def:test-schwartz}
\lean{Rd.testSchwartz, Rd.testSchwartz_apply}
\leanok
For every open $\Omega \subseteq V$ and every test function $\varphi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$,
the complex function
$x \mapsto \varphi(x)$ on $V$ is a Schwartz function, again denoted $\varphi$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Directional derivatives commute]
\label{lem:directional-derivatives-commute}
\lean{LineDeriv.lineDerivOp_iteratedLineDerivOp_comm_of, SchwartzMap.lineDerivOp_comm,
  SchwartzMap.lineDerivOp_iteratedLineDerivOp_comm, Rd.lineDerivOp_testFunction_apply,
  Rd.lineDerivOp_testSchwartz, Rd.iteratedLineDerivOp_testSchwartz,
  Rd.coe_iteratedLineDerivOp_eq, TestFunction.lineDerivOp_comm,
  TestFunction.lineDerivOp_iteratedLineDerivOp_comm}
\leanok
\uses{def:test-schwartz}
For every open $\Omega \subseteq V$, every Schwartz function $u$, every test function
$\varphi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$, all $a, b \in V$ and every $v \in V^k$,
\[
  \partial_a \partial_b u = \partial_b \partial_a u, \quad
  \partial_a \partial^v u = \partial^v \partial_a u, \quad
  \partial_a \partial_b \varphi = \partial_b \partial_a \varphi, \quad
  \partial_a \partial^v \varphi = \partial^v \partial_a \varphi ,
\]
$\partial_a \varphi(x) = D\varphi(x) a$ for every $x \in V$, and $\partial^v \varphi$, as a
Schwartz function, is the iterated derivative $\partial^v$ of the Schwartz function $\varphi$. For
every open $\Omega' \subseteq V$ and every
$\psi \in \mathcal D(\Omega')$ with the same values as $\varphi$, $\partial^v \psi$ and
$\partial^v \varphi$ have the same values.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$\partial_a \partial_b u(x) = D^2 u(x)(a, b)$ is symmetric in $a$ and $b$ because $u$ is $C^2$
(Mathlib's \texttt{ContDiffAt.\allowbreak isSymmSndFDerivAt}). Passing from $\varphi$ to the
complex function $\varphi$ commutes with $\partial_a$, since the derivative of $x \mapsto
\varphi(x) \in \C$ is the derivative of $\varphi$ followed by the inclusion $\R \subseteq \C$; by
induction on $k$ it commutes with $\partial^v$, and the symmetry for $u = \varphi$ gives that of
$\varphi$. A directional derivative commutes with every iterated one by induction on $k$, using
only the commutation of two directional derivatives. The derivatives of $\varphi$ depend only on
its values.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Transpose formula]
\label{lem:distribution-transpose}
\lean{Distribution.iteratedLineDerivOp_apply_apply,
  TemperedDistribution.iteratedLineDerivOp_apply_apply,
  TemperedDistribution.iteratedLineDerivOp_toTemperedDistributionCLM_eq}
\leanok
\uses{lem:directional-derivatives-commute}
For every open $\Omega \subseteq V$, every distribution $T$ on $\Omega$, every tempered
distribution $S$, every $\varphi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$, every Schwartz function $u$ and every
$v \in V^k$,
\[
  \partial^v T(\varphi) = (-1)^k \, T(\partial^v \varphi), \qquad
  \partial^v S(u) = S\bigl((-1)^k \partial^v u\bigr),
\]
and the iterated derivative $\partial^v$ of a Schwartz function $u$ as a tempered distribution
is the tempered distribution of the Schwartz function $\partial^v u$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Induction on $k$: $\partial^v T = \partial_{v_0} \partial^{v'} T$ with
$v' = (v_1, \dots, v_{k-1})$, so
$\partial^v T(\varphi) = \partial^{v'} T(-\partial_{v_0} \varphi)
= (-1)^{k-1} \, T(-\partial^{v'} \partial_{v_0} \varphi)$, and
$\partial^{v'} \partial_{v_0} \varphi = \partial_{v_0} \partial^{v'} \varphi = \partial^v \varphi$
by \Cref{lem:directional-derivatives-commute}. The same induction works for $S$, and for the
Schwartz function $u$ it iterates Mathlib's
\texttt{TemperedDistribution.\allowbreak lineDerivOp\_\allowbreak
toTemperedDistributionCLM\_\allowbreak eq}.
\end{proof}

Tempered distributions are determined by their values on test functions, because the cut-offs
of a Schwartz function converge to it in the topology of $\mathcal S(V)$.

\begin{definition}[Cut-offs of Schwartz functions]
\label{def:schwartz-cutoff}
\lean{Rd.hasCompactSupport_cutoff_smul_mul, Rd.cutoffMul, Rd.cutoffMul_apply,
  Rd.hasCompactSupport_cutoffMul, Rd.cutoffMulBound, Rd.cutoffMulConst, Rd.cutoffMulConst_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{def:lp-kernels, lem:lp-kernels-basic}
For every Schwartz function $u$ and every $N \in \N$, the cut-off of $u$ at radius $N + 1$ is the
smooth compactly supported function
\[
  \chi_N u : x \mapsto \chi_{1,2}\bigl(x / (N + 1)\bigr) \, u(x) .
\]
For all $k, m \in \N$ and $x \in V$ let
\begin{align*}
  B_m(x) &= \|D^m u(x)\| + \sum_{i=0}^m \binom{m}{i} \, p_{0,i}(\chi_{1,2}) \,
  \|D^{m-i} u(x)\|, \\
  C_{k,m}(u) &= p_{k+1,m}(u) + \sum_{i=0}^m \binom{m}{i} \, p_{0,i}(\chi_{1,2}) \,
  p_{k+1,m-i}(u) \geq 0,
\end{align*}
where $p_{k,m}(w) = \sup_x \|x\|^k \|D^m w(x)\|$ are the Schwartz seminorms.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The cut-off estimate]
\label{lem:schwartz-cutoff-estimate}
\lean{Rd.cutoffMul_eventuallyEq, Rd.norm_iteratedFDeriv_cutoff_comp_smul_le,
  Rd.norm_iteratedFDeriv_cutoffMul_le, Rd.norm_iteratedFDeriv_sub_cutoffMul_le,
  Rd.iteratedFDeriv_sub_cutoffMul_eq_zero, Rd.norm_pow_succ_mul_cutoffMulBound_le,
  Rd.seminorm_sub_cutoffMul_le}
\leanok
\uses{def:schwartz-cutoff}
For every Schwartz function $u$ and all $k, m, N \in \N$,
\[
  p_{k,m}(u - \chi_N u) \leq \frac{C_{k,m}(u)}{N + 1} .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
For $0 \leq c \leq 1$, $D^i(\chi_{1,2}(c \,\cdot))(x) = c^i D^i \chi_{1,2}(c x)$ has norm at most
$p_{0,i}(\chi_{1,2})$, so the Leibniz rule (Mathlib's
\texttt{norm\_\allowbreak iteratedFDeriv\_\allowbreak mul\_\allowbreak le}) gives
$\|D^m (u - \chi_N u)(x)\| \leq B_m(x)$ for every $x$. On the open ball of radius $N + 1$ the
cut-off is $1$, so $u - \chi_N u$ vanishes near each of its points and so do all its
derivatives. For $\|x\| \geq N + 1$,
$(N + 1) \|x\|^k B_m(x) \leq \|x\|^{k+1} B_m(x) \leq C_{k,m}(u)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cut-offs converge in the Schwartz space]
\label{lem:schwartz-cutoff-tendsto}
\lean{Rd.tendsto_cutoffMul}
\leanok
\uses{lem:schwartz-cutoff-estimate}
For every Schwartz function $u$, $\chi_N u \to u$ in $\mathcal S(V)$ as $N \to \infty$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The topology of $\mathcal S(V)$ is that of the seminorms $p_{k,m}$ (Mathlib's
\texttt{schwartz\_\allowbreak withSeminorms}), and each $p_{k,m}(\chi_N u - u)$ is at most
$C_{k,m}(u) / (N + 1)$ by \Cref{lem:schwartz-cutoff-estimate}.
\end{proof}

Since every $\chi_N u$ is smooth with compact support, the smooth compactly supported complex
functions are dense in $\mathcal S(V)$.

\begin{theorem}[Test functions determine tempered distributions]
\label{thm:test-functions-determine}
\lean{Rd.exists_testSchwartz_eq, Rd.eq_zero_of_testSchwartz}
\leanok
\uses{lem:schwartz-cutoff-tendsto, def:test-schwartz}
For every complex normed space $F$ and every tempered distribution $T$ with values in $F$ such
that $T(\varphi) = 0$ for every $\varphi \in \mathcal D(V)$, $T = 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Every smooth compactly supported $w : V \to \C$ is $\operatorname{Re} w + i \operatorname{Im} w$
with $\operatorname{Re} w, \operatorname{Im} w \in \mathcal D(V)$, so $T$ vanishes on it by
linearity. For a Schwartz function $u$, $T(\chi_N u) = 0$ for every $N$ and
$T(\chi_N u) \to T(u)$ by \Cref{lem:schwartz-cutoff-tendsto} and the continuity of $T$.
\end{proof}

\section{Weak derivatives on open sets}
\label{sec:weak-derivatives}

Throughout this section $\Omega \subseteq V$ is open. Mathlib identifies a locally integrable
function $f$ on $\Omega$ with the distribution $\varphi \mapsto \int \varphi f$ and a function
$f \in L_p(V)$, $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, with the tempered distribution $u \mapsto \int u f$.

\begin{definition}[Weak derivatives and Sobolev spaces]
\label{def:weak-line-derivative}
\lean{Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv, Rd.MemWeakSobolev, Rd.MemSobolev}
\leanok
For every $v \in V^k$, $g$ is the weak derivative $\partial^v f$ of $f$ on $\Omega$ if $f$ and $g$
are locally integrable on $\Omega$ and $\partial^v f = g$ as distributions on $\Omega$. For every
$m \in \N$ and every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, $f$ lies in the Sobolev space $\Sob{m}{p}(\Omega)$ if
$f \in L_p(\Omega)$ and for every $k \leq m$ and every $v \in V^k$ the weak derivative
$\partial^v f$ exists on $\Omega$ and lies in $L_p(\Omega)$. For every $f \in L_p(V)$,
$f \in \Sob{m}{p}(V)$ means $f \in \Sob{m}{p}(\Omega)$ with $\Omega = V$.
\end{definition}

Every function in $L_p(\Omega)$ with $p \geq 1$ is locally integrable on $\Omega$
(\Cref{lem:weak-derivative-basic}), so the weak derivatives in the definition of
$\Sob{m}{p}(\Omega)$ need no further hypothesis. The definition quantifies over all directions;
a basis of $V$ enters only in proofs.

\begin{lemma}[Weak derivatives by integration by parts]
\label{lem:weak-derivative-integral}
\lean{Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.integral_eq, Rd.hasWeakLineDeriv_iff_integral}
\leanok
\uses{def:weak-line-derivative, lem:distribution-transpose}
For all locally integrable $f$, $g$ on $\Omega$ and every $v \in V^k$, $g$ is the weak
derivative $\partial^v f$ on $\Omega$ if and only if for every $\varphi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$,
\[
  \int_V \varphi \, g = (-1)^k \int_V (\partial^v \varphi) \, f .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Both distributions are determined by their values on test functions, the distribution of a
locally integrable function is $\varphi \mapsto \int \varphi f$ (Mathlib's
\texttt{Distribution.\allowbreak ofFun\_\allowbreak apply}), and
$\partial^v f(\varphi) = (-1)^k f(\partial^v \varphi)$ by \Cref{lem:distribution-transpose}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Properties of weak derivatives]
\label{lem:weak-derivative-basic}
\lean{Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.unique, Rd.hasWeakLineDeriv_fin_zero, Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.add,
  Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.neg, Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.sub, Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.smul,
  Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.congr_ae, Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.mono, Rd.hasWeakLineDeriv_zero,
  Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.ae_eq_zero_of_ae_eq_zero,
  Rd.locallyIntegrableOn_of_memLp, Rd.memWeakSobolev_zero_iff, Rd.MemWeakSobolev.mono_order,
  Rd.MemWeakSobolev.mono_set, Rd.zero_memWeakSobolev, Rd.MemWeakSobolev.add,
  Rd.MemWeakSobolev.smul, Rd.MemWeakSobolev.congr_ae, Rd.zero_memSobolev, Rd.MemSobolev.add,
  Rd.MemSobolev.smul, Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.sum, Rd.memSobolev_iff_exists_hasWeakLineDeriv,
  Rd.MemSobolev.sum, Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.eq_of_top, Rd.memSobolev_one_of_forall_hasWeakLineDeriv}
\leanok
\uses{def:weak-line-derivative, lem:weak-derivative-integral, lem:directional-derivatives-commute}
For every $v \in V^k$, all functions $f, f', g, g'$ and every $c \in \C$:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item if $g$ and $g'$ are weak derivatives $\partial^v f$ on $\Omega$, then $g = g'$ almost
    everywhere on $\Omega$; for $\Omega = V$, every $r \in [0, \infty]$ and
    $g, g' \in L_r(V)$, $g = g'$ in $L_r(V)$;
  \item for $k = 0$, every locally integrable $f$ on $\Omega$ is its own weak derivative;
  \item if $g = \partial^v f$ and $g' = \partial^v f'$ weakly on $\Omega$, then
    $g + g' = \partial^v (f + f')$, $-g = \partial^v(-f)$, $g - g' = \partial^v (f - f')$ and
    $c g = \partial^v (c f)$ weakly on $\Omega$; for a finite set $s$ and functions $F_j$,
    $G_j$ with $G_j = \partial^v F_j$ weakly on $\Omega$ for every $j \in s$,
    $\sum_{j \in s} G_j = \partial^v \sum_{j \in s} F_j$ weakly on $\Omega$;
  \item if $g = \partial^v f$ weakly on $\Omega$, $f = f'$ and $g = g'$ almost everywhere on
    $\Omega$, then $g' = \partial^v f'$ weakly on $\Omega$;
  \item if $g = \partial^v f$ weakly on $\Omega$, then $g = \partial^v f$ weakly on every open
    $\Omega' \subseteq \Omega$;
  \item $0 = \partial^v 0$ weakly on $\Omega$;
  \item if $g = \partial^v f$ weakly on $\Omega$, $O \subseteq \Omega$ is open and $f = 0$
    almost everywhere on $O$, then $g = 0$ almost everywhere on $O$.
\end{enumerate}
For every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, every $f \in L_p(\Omega)$ is locally integrable on $\Omega$
and $\Sob{0}{p}(\Omega) = L_p(\Omega)$. For all $m, l \in \N$ with
$l \leq m$, every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ and every open $\Omega' \subseteq \Omega$,
$\Sob{m}{p}(\Omega) \subseteq \Sob{l}{p}(\Omega)$, every $f \in \Sob{m}{p}(\Omega)$ lies in
$\Sob{m}{p}(\Omega')$, and $\Sob{m}{p}(\Omega)$ is a complex vector space. For every
$f \in \Sob{m}{p}(\Omega)$ and every $f'$ with $f' = f$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$,
$f' \in \Sob{m}{p}(\Omega)$. For $\Omega = V$, $\Sob{m}{p}(V)$ is a complex linear subspace of
$L_p(V)$, and $f \in L_p(V)$ lies in $\Sob{m}{p}(V)$ if and only if for every $k \leq m$ and
every $v \in V^k$ some $g \in L_p(V)$ is the weak derivative $\partial^v f$ on $V$; for $m = 1$
it suffices that for every $v \in V$ some $g \in L_p(V)$ is the weak derivative $\partial_v f$
on $V$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
(1) A locally integrable function is determined almost everywhere on $\Omega$ by its
distribution (Mathlib's \texttt{Distribution.\allowbreak ofFun\_\allowbreak injective}). (2)
$\partial^v$ is the identity for $k = 0$. (3) The distribution of a function and $\partial^v$ are
additive, and finite sums follow by induction; for complex $c$ use
\Cref{lem:weak-derivative-integral}, since $c$ leaves both integrals. (4) The distribution of a
function depends on it only almost everywhere on $\Omega$.
(5) A test function $\varphi$ on $\Omega'$ is one on $\Omega$, with the same derivatives
(\Cref{lem:directional-derivatives-commute}), so the identity of
\Cref{lem:weak-derivative-integral} on $\Omega$ gives it on $\Omega'$. (6) The distribution of
$0$ is $0$, and so are its derivatives. (7) By (5) and (4), $g = \partial^v 0$ weakly on $O$,
so $g = 0$ almost everywhere on $O$ by (6) and (1). A function in $L_p(\Omega)$, $p \geq 1$, is
integrable on every compact subset of $\Omega$, which has finite measure. The statements on
$\Sob{m}{p}$ follow, with $L_p(\Omega') \supseteq L_p(\Omega)|_{\Omega'}$ and (4); in $L_p(V)$,
the zero class, and the class of a sum or a multiple, agree almost everywhere with $0$ and with
the sum or the multiple of the representatives, and a weak derivative in $L_p(V)$ may be
replaced by its class (4). For $m = 1$ the order $k = 0$ is (2).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Complex test functions]
\label{lem:weak-derivative-complex-test}
\lean{Rd.exists_testSchwartz_eq_of_tsupport_subset, Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.integral_mul_eq}
\leanok
\uses{lem:weak-derivative-integral, def:test-schwartz, lem:directional-derivatives-commute}
Every smooth compactly supported $w \colon V \to \C$ with support in $\Omega$ is
$w = a + i b$ for real test functions $a, b \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$. For every $v \in V^k$, all
$f$, $g$ with $g = \partial^v f$ weakly on $\Omega$ and every such $w$,
\[
  \int_V w \, g = (-1)^k \int_V (\partial^v w) \, f .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Take $a = \operatorname{Re} w$ and $b = \operatorname{Im} w$, whose supports lie in that of $w$.
Then $\partial^v w = \partial^v a + i \, \partial^v b$
(\Cref{lem:directional-derivatives-commute}), and \Cref{lem:weak-derivative-integral} for $a$ and
$b$ gives the identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The product rule for weak derivatives]
\label{lem:weak-derivative-product}
\lean{Rd.testFunctionMul, Rd.testFunctionMul_apply, Rd.lineDerivOp_testFunctionMul_apply,
  Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.mul_contDiff}
\leanok
\uses{lem:weak-derivative-integral}
For every test function $\varphi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$ and every smooth real function $\chi$
on $V$, $\varphi \chi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$ with
$\partial_w (\varphi \chi) = (\partial_w \varphi) \chi + \varphi \, \partial_w \chi$. For every
$w \in V$, all $f$, $g$ with $g = \partial_w f$ weakly on $\Omega$ and every smooth real $\chi$,
$\chi g + (\partial_w \chi) f = \partial_w (\chi f)$ weakly on $\Omega$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The products of $\chi$ and $\partial_w \chi$ with locally integrable functions on $\Omega$ are
locally integrable on $\Omega$. For $\varphi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$,
\[
  \int \varphi \bigl(\chi g + (\partial_w \chi) f\bigr) = -\int \partial_w(\varphi \chi) \, f
  + \int \varphi \, (\partial_w \chi) f = -\int (\partial_w \varphi) \, \chi f
\]
by \Cref{lem:weak-derivative-integral} for the test function $\varphi \chi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pairing with a test function]
\label{lem:test-function-pairing}
\lean{Rd.eLpNorm_testFunction_smul_le, Rd.eventually_memLp_of_tendsto,
  Rd.tendsto_integral_testFunction_smul}
\leanok
For every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, every $\varphi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$ with support $K$ and
every $h$ that is almost everywhere strongly measurable on $\Omega$,
\[
  \|\varphi h\|_{L_1(\Omega)} \leq \|\varphi\|_\infty \, |K|^{1 - 1/p} \, \|h\|_{L_p(\Omega)} .
\]
For every filter, every $h \in L_p(\Omega)$ and all $h_i$ with
$\|h_i - h\|_{L_p(\Omega)} \to 0$, eventually $h_i \in L_p(\Omega)$ and
$\int_V \varphi h_i \to \int_V \varphi h$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$\varphi h$ vanishes off the compact set $K \subseteq \Omega$, so its $L_1(\Omega)$ norm is that on
$K$, which is at most $|K|^{1 - 1/p}$ times its $L_p(K)$ norm (H\"older's inequality on the set
$K$ of finite measure), and $\|\varphi h\|_{L_p(K)} \leq \|\varphi\|_\infty \|h\|_{L_p(\Omega)}$.
Eventually $\|h_i - h\|_{L_p(\Omega)} < 1$, and then $h_i = (h_i - h) + h \in L_p(\Omega)$. The
integrals over $V$ are integrals over $\Omega$, and the bound applied to $h_i - h$ gives the
convergence in $L_1(\Omega)$ of $\varphi h_i$ to $\varphi h$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Weak derivatives pass to limits]
\label{thm:weak-derivative-limits}
\lean{Rd.HasWeakLineDeriv.of_tendsto}
\leanok
\uses{lem:weak-derivative-integral, lem:test-function-pairing}
For all $1 \leq p, r \leq \infty$, every $v \in V^k$, every nontrivial filter, every
$f \in L_p(\Omega)$, every $g \in L_r(\Omega)$ and all $f_i$, $g_i$ with $g_i = \partial^v f_i$
weakly on $\Omega$ for every $i$, $\|f_i - f\|_{L_p(\Omega)} \to 0$ and
$\|g_i - g\|_{L_r(\Omega)} \to 0$, $g$ is the weak derivative $\partial^v f$ on $\Omega$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
For every $\varphi \in \mathcal D(\Omega)$,
$\int \varphi g_i = (-1)^k \int (\partial^v \varphi) f_i$ by
\Cref{lem:weak-derivative-integral}; both sides converge by \Cref{lem:test-function-pairing},
to $\int \varphi g$ and to $(-1)^k \int (\partial^v \varphi) f$, and limits in $\C$ are unique.
\end{proof}

The bridge to tempered distributions rests on \Cref{thm:test-functions-determine}. For
$1 \leq p \leq \infty$ and $f \in L_p(V)$ let $T_f$ be $f$ as a distribution on $V$ and
$S_f$ be $f$ as a tempered distribution.

\begin{lemma}[$L_p$ functions as distributions on $V$]
\label{lem:lp-distribution-whole-space}
\lean{Rd.volume_restrict_top, Rd.locallyIntegrableOn_top_Lp, Rd.ofFun_top_apply,
  Rd.iteratedLineDerivOp_ofFun_top_apply}
\leanok
\uses{lem:distribution-transpose, def:test-schwartz, lem:directional-derivatives-commute,
  lem:weak-derivative-basic}
Lebesgue measure restricted to $\Omega = V$ is Lebesgue measure, so $L_p(\Omega) = L_p(V)$. For
every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, every $f \in L_p(V)$, every $\varphi \in \mathcal D(V)$ and
every $v \in V^k$, $f$ is locally integrable on $V$, and
\[
  T_f(\varphi) = S_f(\varphi), \qquad \partial^v T_f(\varphi) = \partial^v S_f(\varphi),
\]
with $\varphi$ as a Schwartz function on the right.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Both sides of the first identity are $\int \varphi f$. For the second, both sides are
$(-1)^k \int (\partial^v \varphi) f$ by \Cref{lem:distribution-transpose}, since the Schwartz
function $\partial^v \varphi$ is the iterated derivative of the Schwartz function $\varphi$
(\Cref{lem:directional-derivatives-commute}).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Weak derivatives are derivatives of tempered distributions]
\label{thm:weak-derivative-tempered}
\lean{Rd.hasWeakLineDeriv_top_iff}
\leanok
\uses{lem:lp-distribution-whole-space, thm:test-functions-determine, def:weak-line-derivative}
For all $1 \leq p, r \leq \infty$, every $f \in L_p(V)$, every $g \in L_r(V)$ and every
$v \in V^k$, $g$ is the weak derivative $\partial^v f$ on $V$ if and only if $\partial^v f = g$
as tempered distributions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
By \Cref{lem:lp-distribution-whole-space} the distribution $\partial^v T_f - T_g$ on $V$ and the
tempered distribution $\partial^v S_f - S_g$ agree on test functions. If the tempered distribution
is zero, so is the distribution. If the distribution is zero, the tempered distribution vanishes
on test functions and is zero by \Cref{thm:test-functions-determine}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sobolev spaces by tempered distributions]
\label{cor:sobolev-tempered}
\lean{Rd.memSobolev_iff_tempered}
\leanok
\uses{thm:weak-derivative-tempered, lem:weak-derivative-basic}
For every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, every $m \in \N$ and every $f \in L_p(V)$, $f \in \Sob{m}{p}(V)$
if and only if for every $k \leq m$ and every $v \in V^k$ there is $g \in L_p(V)$ with
$\partial^v f = g$ as tempered distributions.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\Cref{thm:weak-derivative-tempered}, with a function in $L_p(V)$ replaced by its class, which
changes it only on a null set (\Cref{lem:weak-derivative-basic}).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Schwartz functions]
\label{cor:weak-derivative-schwartz}
\lean{Rd.iteratedLineDerivOp_toLp_eq, Rd.hasWeakLineDeriv_schwartz, Rd.memSobolev_toLp}
\leanok
\uses{lem:distribution-transpose, thm:weak-derivative-tempered, cor:sobolev-tempered,
  lem:weak-derivative-basic}
For every Schwartz function $\eta$, every $v \in V^k$ and every open $\Omega \subseteq V$, the
classical derivative $\partial^v \eta$ is the weak derivative of $\eta$ on $\Omega$. For every
$1 \leq p \leq \infty$ and every $m \in \N$, $\eta \in \Sob{m}{p}(V)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
As tempered distributions $\partial^v \eta$ is the Schwartz function $\partial^v \eta$
(\Cref{lem:distribution-transpose}); \Cref{thm:weak-derivative-tempered} with $p = r = 2$ gives
the weak derivative on $V$, and \Cref{lem:weak-derivative-basic} (5) on $\Omega$. The Sobolev
statement is \Cref{cor:sobolev-tempered} with $g = \partial^v \eta$.
\end{proof}

\section{Mathlib's Sobolev spaces \texorpdfstring{$H^s$}{H\^{}s} by Littlewood--Paley blocks}
\label{sec:sobolev-two-littlewood-paley}

Mathlib defines the Bessel potential $J_s u = \mathcal F^{-1}(\langle \xi \rangle^s \widehat u)$ of
a tempered distribution $u$, with $\langle \xi \rangle^s = (1 + |\xi|^2)^{s/2}$, and the Sobolev
space $H^s(V)$ of the tempered distributions $u$ with $J_s u \in L_2(V)$
(\texttt{TemperedDistribution.\allowbreak besselPotential},
\texttt{TemperedDistribution.\allowbreak MemSobolev}; the bundled space is
\texttt{BesselPotentialSpace}). This section identifies $H^s(V)$, $s \geq 0$, with the
Triebel--Lizorkin space $\TL{s}{2}{2}$ of \Cref{def:triebel-lizorkin} and, for $s > 0$, with the
Besov space $\Besov{s}{2}{2}$, with explicit constants, and proves $\Sob{1}{2}(V) = H^1(V)$. The
Fourier transform $\widehat F$ of $F \in L_2(V)$ is Plancherel's, Mathlib's linear isometry of
$L_2(V)$, and Mathlib identifies it with the Fourier transform of the tempered distribution of
$F$ (\texttt{Lp.\allowbreak fourier\_\allowbreak toTemperedDistribution\_\allowbreak eq}).

\begin{lemma}[Plancherel's theorem]
\label{lem:plancherel-l2}
\lean{Rd.two_ne_top, Rd.enorm_fourier_Lp_two, Rd.enorm_sq_eq_lintegral,
  Rd.lintegral_enorm_sq_eq_enorm_toLp}
\leanok
In $[0, \infty]$, $2 \neq \infty$. For every $F \in L_2(V)$, $\|\widehat F\|_2 = \|F\|_2$. On
every measure space, $\|F\|_2^2 = \int |F|^2$ for every $F \in L_2$, and
$\int |f|^2 = \|[f]\|_2^2$ for every measurable function $f$ with $\int |f|^2 < \infty$ and its
class $[f] \in L_2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The Fourier transform on $L_2(V)$ is a linear isometry in Mathlib
(\texttt{Lp.\allowbreak norm\_\allowbreak fourier\_\allowbreak eq}), in particular continuous
(\texttt{FourierTransform.\allowbreak continuous\_\allowbreak fourier}). The third identity is
the definition of the $L_2$ norm, and the last one is the third for $F = [f]$, since $[f] = f$
almost everywhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[$L_p$ functions as tempered distributions]
\label{lem:lp-distribution-determined}
\lean{Rd.eq_of_toTemperedDistribution_eq}
\leanok
For every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, all $f, g \in L_p(V)$ with the same tempered distribution are
equal.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Mathlib's \texttt{Lp.\allowbreak ker\_\allowbreak toTemperedDistributionCLM\_\allowbreak
eq\_\allowbreak bot}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The norm of Mathlib's $H^{s,p}$]
\label{lem:bessel-space-enorm}
\lean{BesselPotentialSpace.enorm_toLp_eq}
\leanok
For every $s \in \R$, every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ and every $U \in H^{s,p}(V)$,
$\|J_s U\|_p = \|U\|$ in $[0, \infty]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Mathlib's \texttt{BesselPotentialSpace.\allowbreak norm\_\allowbreak toLp\_\allowbreak eq}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The convolution theorem on $L_2$]
\label{thm:convolution-theorem-l2}
\lean{Rd.fourier_convLp_toLp, Rd.fourier_convLp, Rd.enorm_convLp_sq, Rd.fourier_lpBlock,
  Rd.enorm_lpBlock_sq}
\leanok
\uses{lem:fourier-integrable, lem:fourier-conv, lem:plancherel-l2, lem:conv-op, def:lp-blocks,
  lem:lp-kernels-basic, lem:lp-distribution-determined}
For every integrable $K$ on $V$ and every $f \in L_2(V)$,
$\widehat{K * f} = \widehat K \, \widehat f$ almost everywhere and
\[
  \|K * f\|_2^2 = \int_V |\widehat K(\xi)|^2 \, |\widehat f(\xi)|^2 \, d\xi .
\]
In particular, for every $f \in L_2(V)$ and every $j \in \N$,
$\widehat{\Delta_j f} = \widehat{\psi_j} \, \widehat f$ almost everywhere and
\[
  \|\Delta_j f\|_2^2 = \int_V |\widehat{\psi_j}(\xi)|^2 \, |\widehat f(\xi)|^2 \, d\xi .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Let first $f = \varphi$ be a Schwartz function. Then $K * \varphi$ is integrable, and for every
Schwartz function $u$, by \Cref{lem:fourier-integrable} and
$\widehat{K * \varphi} = \widehat K \, \widehat \varphi$ for integrable functions
(\Cref{lem:fourier-conv}),
\[
  \int \widehat u \, (K * \varphi) = \int u \, \widehat{K * \varphi}
  = \int u \, \widehat K \, \widehat \varphi .
\]
The left side is the Fourier transform of the tempered distribution of $K * \varphi$ applied to
$u$, which is the tempered distribution of the $L_2$ Fourier transform of $K * \varphi$ applied
to $u$. So the tempered distributions of the $L_2$ functions $\widehat{K * \varphi}$ and
$\widehat K \, \widehat \varphi$ agree, and an $L_2$ function is determined by its tempered
distribution (\Cref{lem:lp-distribution-determined}). Both sides of the identity are continuous
in $f \in L_2(V)$: the left by
Young's inequality (\Cref{lem:conv-op}) and \Cref{lem:plancherel-l2}, the right because
$\widehat K \in L_\infty$ (\Cref{lem:fourier-integrable}). Schwartz functions are dense in
$L_2(V)$, so the identity holds for all $f$. The norm identity follows with
\Cref{lem:plancherel-l2}, and the statements on the blocks are the case $K = \psi_j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[The Bessel weight]
\label{def:bessel-weight}
\lean{Rd.besselWeight}
\leanok
For $s \in \R$ and $\xi \in V$, $\langle \xi \rangle^s = (1 + |\xi|^2)^{s/2}$.
\end{definition}

The Bessel weight is the symbol of Mathlib's Bessel potential $J_s$:
$\widehat{J_s u} = \langle \cdot \rangle^s \widehat u$.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary properties of the weights]
\label{lem:bessel-weight-basic}
\lean{Rd.besselWeight_nonneg, Rd.besselWeight_neg, Rd.hasTemperateGrowth_besselWeight,
  Rd.enorm_besselWeight, Rd.ofReal_besselWeight_sq, Rd.norm_le_besselWeight_one,
  ENNReal.dyadicWeight_sq, Rd.one_add_norm_sq_le_of_norm_lt}
\leanok
\uses{def:bessel-weight, def:lq-norm}
For every $s \in \R$, the Bessel weight $\xi \mapsto \langle \xi \rangle^s$ is nonnegative, even
and smooth with polynomially bounded derivatives, $(\langle \xi \rangle^s)^2 = (1 + |\xi|^2)^s$ and
$|\xi| \leq \langle \xi \rangle^1$ for every $\xi \in V$, and $(2^{js})^2 = (4^j)^s$ for every
$j \in \N$. For every $j \in \N$ and every $\xi \in V$ with $|\xi| < 2^{j+1}$,
$1 + |\xi|^2 \leq 5 \cdot 4^j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The weight depends on $|\xi|$ only, and the smoothness and the growth bounds of
$(1 + |\xi|^2)^{s/2}$ are in Mathlib. Further, $|\xi|^2 < 4^{j+1} = 4 \cdot 4^j$ and
$1 \leq 4^j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[The Bessel potential on Schwartz functions]
\label{def:bessel-schwartz}
\lean{Rd.besselSchwartz}
\leanok
\uses{def:bessel-weight, lem:bessel-weight-basic}
For $t \in \R$ and a Schwartz function $u$,
$J_t u = \mathcal F^{-1}(\langle \cdot \rangle^t \widehat u)$, a continuous linear map of the
Schwartz space.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[$J_t$ on Schwartz functions and on distributions]
\label{lem:bessel-schwartz-distribution}
\lean{Rd.besselPotential_schwartz, Rd.besselSchwartz_apply,
  Rd.besselSchwartz_besselSchwartz_neg}
\leanok
\uses{def:bessel-schwartz}
For every $t \in \R$ and every Schwartz function $u$, the tempered distribution of $J_t u$ is
Mathlib's $J_t$ of the tempered distribution of $u$,
$J_t u(x) = \mathcal F^{-1}(\langle \cdot \rangle^t \widehat u)(x)$ for every $x \in V$, with the
Fourier integrals of functions, and $J_t J_{-t} u = u$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Mathlib's
\texttt{TemperedDistribution.\allowbreak fourierMultiplierCLM\_\allowbreak
toTemperedDistributionCLM\_\allowbreak eq}; the composition of two Fourier multipliers is the
multiplier of the product of their symbols, here
$\langle \xi \rangle^t \langle \xi \rangle^{-t} = 1$.
\end{proof}

For a function $m$ on $V$ that is smooth with polynomially bounded derivatives,
$m(D) u = \mathcal F^{-1}(m \, \widehat u)$ is Mathlib's Fourier multiplier on Schwartz functions
and on tempered distributions (\texttt{SchwartzMap.\allowbreak fourier\allowbreak MultiplierCLM},
\texttt{TemperedDistribution.\allowbreak fourier\allowbreak MultiplierCLM}); $J_t$ is the case
$m = \langle \cdot \rangle^t$. Mathlib lets $m(D)$ act on a tempered distribution $T$ by
$(m(D) T)(u) = T\bigl(\mathcal F(m \, \mathcal F^{-1} u)\bigr)$. The symbol $m$ is even if
$m(-\xi) = m(\xi)$ for every $\xi \in V$.

\begin{lemma}[Even Fourier multipliers act by the transpose]
\label{lem:even-multiplier-transpose}
\lean{Rd.fourierMultiplierCLM_apply_eq_fourier, Rd.fourierMultiplierCLM_apply_apply_of_even}
\leanok
\uses{lem:bessel-schwartz-distribution}
Let $m$ be an even function on $V$, smooth with polynomially bounded derivatives. For every
Schwartz function $u$ and every $x \in V$,
$m(D) u(x) = \mathcal F(m \, \mathcal F^{-1} u)(x)$, and for every tempered distribution $T$,
$(m(D) T)(u) = T(m(D) u)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$\mathcal F^{-1} h(x) = \widehat{h}(-x)$ and $\mathcal F^{-1} u(\xi) = \widehat u(-\xi)$ (Mathlib's
\texttt{Real.\allowbreak fourierInv\_\allowbreak eq\_\allowbreak fourier\_\allowbreak
comp\_\allowbreak neg}), so
$m(D) u(x) = \mathcal F(m(-\cdot) \, \widehat u(-\cdot))(x) = \mathcal F(m \, \mathcal F^{-1} u)(x)$
since $m$ is even. The second identity is Mathlib's definition of $m(D) T$ with the first.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The transpose of the Bessel potential]
\label{lem:bessel-potential-transpose}
\lean{Rd.besselSchwartz_apply_eq_fourier, Rd.besselPotential_apply_apply,
  Rd.integral_besselSchwartz_mul}
\leanok
\uses{def:bessel-schwartz, lem:bessel-weight-basic, lem:bessel-schwartz-distribution,
  lem:even-multiplier-transpose}
For every $t \in \R$, every Schwartz function $u$ and every $x \in V$,
$J_t u(x) = \mathcal F(\langle \cdot \rangle^t \, \mathcal F^{-1} u)(x)$. For every $t \in \R$,
every tempered distribution $T$ and all Schwartz functions $\varphi, u$,
\[
  (J_t T)(u) = T(J_t u) \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  \int_V J_t \varphi \, u = \int_V \varphi \, J_t u .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The Bessel weight is even (\Cref{lem:bessel-weight-basic}), so \Cref{lem:even-multiplier-transpose}
gives the first two identities. For the tempered distribution of $\varphi$ the second gives
$\int_V J_t u \, \varphi = (J_t \varphi)(u) = \int_V u \, J_t \varphi$
(\Cref{lem:bessel-schwartz-distribution}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two elementary inequalities]
\label{lem:elementary-square-inequalities}
\lean{Rd.one_le_two_mul_enorm_sq_add, Rd.le_rpow_half_mul_of_sq_le}
\leanok
For all $x, y \in \C$ with $x + y = 1$, $1 \leq 2(|x|^2 + |y|^2)$. For all
$a, b, c \in [0, \infty]$ with $a^2 \leq c \, b^2$, $a \leq c^{1/2} \, b$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$1 \leq |x| + |y|$ by the triangle inequality, and $(|x| + |y|)^2 \leq 2(|x|^2 + |y|^2)$
(Mathlib's \texttt{add\_\allowbreak sq\_\allowbreak le}); and $(c^{1/2} b)^2 = c \, b^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The Bessel weight and the Littlewood--Paley weights]
\label{prop:bessel-lp-weights}
\lean{Rd.dyadicWeight_sq_le_of_fourier_psi_ne_zero, Rd.ofReal_besselWeight_sq_le_of_norm_lt,
  Rd.tsum_dyadicWeight_fourier_psi_sq_le, Rd.ofReal_besselWeight_sq_le_tsum}
\leanok
\uses{lem:bessel-weight-basic, lem:elementary-square-inequalities, lem:fourier-psi-window}
For every $s \geq 0$, every $j \in \N$ and every $\xi \in V$: if $\widehat{\psi_j}(\xi) \neq 0$,
then $2^{2js} \leq 4^s \langle \xi \rangle^{2s}$; if $|\xi| < 2^{j+1}$, then
$\langle \xi \rangle^{2s} \leq 5^s \, 2^{2js}$; and
\[
  \sum_{j \in \N} 2^{2js} |\widehat{\psi_j}(\xi)|^2 \leq 2 \cdot 4^s \langle \xi \rangle^{2s},
  \qquad
  \langle \xi \rangle^{2s} \leq 2 \cdot 5^s \sum_{j \in \N} 2^{2js} |\widehat{\psi_j}(\xi)|^2 .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The first two bounds are $(4^j)^s \leq (4(1 + |\xi|^2))^s$ and
$(1 + |\xi|^2)^s \leq (5 \cdot 4^j)^s$ (\Cref{lem:fourier-psi-window,lem:bessel-weight-basic}),
using $s \geq 0$. Let $a$ be as in \Cref{lem:fourier-psi-window}. The sum has at most the two
terms $j = a, a + 1$, each at most $4^s \langle \xi \rangle^{2s}$, since
$|\widehat{\psi_j}(\xi)| \leq 1$. Both $j = a$ and $j = a + 1$ satisfy $|\xi| < 2^{j+1}$, and
$1 \leq 2 (|\widehat{\psi_a}(\xi)|^2 + |\widehat{\psi_{a+1}}(\xi)|^2)$ by
\Cref{lem:elementary-square-inequalities}, so
$\langle \xi \rangle^{2s} \leq 2 \sum_{j \in \{a, a+1\}} \langle \xi \rangle^{2s}
|\widehat{\psi_j}(\xi)|^2 \leq 2 \cdot 5^s \sum_{j \in \{a, a+1\}} 2^{2js}
|\widehat{\psi_j}(\xi)|^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Temperate weights and $L_p$ functions]
\label{lem:temperate-weight-lp}
\lean{Rd.smulLeftCLM_toTemperedDistribution_eq, Rd.ae_eq_of_smulLeftCLM_eq}
\leanok
Let $w$ be a smooth function on $V$ with polynomially bounded derivatives, and
$1 \leq p, q \leq \infty$. For every $g \in L_p(V)$ with $w g \in L_q(V)$, the product of $w$
with the tempered distribution of $g$ is the tempered distribution of $w g$. For every
$G \in L_p(V)$ and every $H \in L_q(V)$ such that $w G = H$ as tempered distributions,
$w G = H$ almost everywhere.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Both distributions in the first statement send a Schwartz function $u$ to $\int u \, w g$. In
the second, $w G$ and $H$ are locally integrable, and testing with the Schwartz functions
$\varphi \in C^\infty_c(V)$ gives $\int \varphi \, w G = \int \varphi \, H$; such functions
are equal almost everywhere (Mathlib's \texttt{ae\_\allowbreak eq\_\allowbreak of\_\allowbreak
integral\_\allowbreak contDiff\_\allowbreak smul\_\allowbreak eq}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Bessel potentials of $L_2$ functions]
\label{lem:bessel-potential-l2}
\lean{Rd.fourier_ae_eq_of_besselPotential_eq, Rd.enorm_sq_eq_lintegral_of_besselPotential_eq,
  Rd.memLp_besselWeight_mul_fourier, Rd.memSobolev_two_of_lintegral_lt_top,
  Rd.exists_toTemperedDistribution_eq_of_besselPotential_eq}
\leanok
\uses{def:bessel-weight, lem:bessel-weight-basic, lem:temperate-weight-lp, lem:plancherel-l2}
Let $s \in \R$. For all $f, h \in L_2(V)$ with $J_s f = h$, $\widehat h = \langle \cdot \rangle^s
\widehat f$ almost everywhere and
\[
  \|h\|_2^2 = \int_V \langle \xi \rangle^{2s} |\widehat f(\xi)|^2 \, d\xi .
\]
For every $f \in L_2(V)$ with $\int \langle \xi \rangle^{2s} |\widehat f(\xi)|^2 \, d\xi < \infty$,
$\langle \cdot \rangle^s \widehat f \in L_2(V)$ and $f \in H^s(V)$. If $s \geq 0$, then every
tempered distribution $u$ with $J_s u \in L_2(V)$ is an $L_2(V)$ function.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The Fourier transform of $J_s f$ is $\langle \cdot \rangle^s \widehat f$ as tempered
distributions, so the first identity is \Cref{lem:temperate-weight-lp}, and the second follows by
\Cref{lem:plancherel-l2}. In the second statement, $\langle \cdot \rangle^s \widehat f$ is the
Fourier transform of $J_s f$ by \Cref{lem:temperate-weight-lp}, so $J_s f$ is the inverse Fourier
transform of an $L_2$ function (Mathlib's \texttt{TemperedDistribution.\allowbreak
memSobolev\_\allowbreak iff\_\allowbreak exists\_\allowbreak smulLeftCLM\_\allowbreak fourier}).
For the third, $u = J_{-s}(J_s u)$, and $J_{-s}$ maps $L_2(V) = H^0(V)$ into $L_2(V)$ for
$-s \leq 0$ (Mathlib's \texttt{TemperedDistribution.\allowbreak MemSobolev.\allowbreak mono}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The Triebel--Lizorkin norm of $\TL{s}{2}{2}$ on the frequency side]
\label{lem:tl-two-fourier}
\lean{Rd.triebelLizorkinNorm_two_sq, Rd.triebelLizorkinNorm_two_sq_le,
  Rd.lintegral_besselWeight_sq_le}
\leanok
\uses{def:triebel-lizorkin, thm:tl-diagonal, thm:convolution-theorem-l2,
  prop:bessel-lp-weights}
For every $s \in \R$ and every $f \in L_2(V)$,
\[
  \|f\|_{F^s_{2,2}}^2 = \int_V \Bigl( \sum_{j \in \N} 2^{2js} |\widehat{\psi_j}(\xi)|^2 \Bigr)
  |\widehat f(\xi)|^2 \, d\xi ,
\]
and if $s \geq 0$, then
$\|f\|_{F^s_{2,2}}^2 \leq 2 \cdot 4^s \int_V \langle \xi \rangle^{2s} |\widehat f(\xi)|^2 \, d\xi$
and $\int_V \langle \xi \rangle^{2s} |\widehat f(\xi)|^2 \, d\xi \leq 2 \cdot 5^s
\|f\|_{F^s_{2,2}}^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
By \Cref{thm:tl-diagonal}, $\|f\|_{F^s_{2,2}}^2 = \sum_j 2^{2js} \|\Delta_j f\|_2^2$; insert
\Cref{thm:convolution-theorem-l2} and interchange sum and integral (Tonelli). The bounds follow
from \Cref{prop:bessel-lp-weights} under the integral.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$H^s = \TL{s}{2}{2}$]
\label{thm:sobolev-two-triebel-lizorkin}
\lean{Rd.triebelLizorkinNorm_le_of_besselPotential_eq,
  Rd.enorm_besselPotential_le_triebelLizorkinNorm, Rd.memSobolev_two_iff_memTriebelLizorkin}
\leanok
\uses{lem:bessel-potential-l2, lem:tl-two-fourier, lem:elementary-square-inequalities}
For every $s \geq 0$ and all $f, h \in L_2(V)$ with $J_s f = h$,
\[
  \|f\|_{F^s_{2,2}} \leq (2 \cdot 4^s)^{1/2} \, \|h\|_2
  \quad \text{and} \quad
  \|h\|_2 \leq (2 \cdot 5^s)^{1/2} \, \|f\|_{F^s_{2,2}} .
\]
For every $s \geq 0$, a tempered distribution $u$ lies in $H^s(V)$ if and only if $u$ is a
function $f \in L_2(V)$ with $f \in \TL{s}{2}{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
By \Cref{lem:bessel-potential-l2}, $\|h\|_2^2 = \int \langle \xi \rangle^{2s} |\widehat f|^2$,
and \Cref{lem:tl-two-fourier} gives both bounds after taking square roots
(\Cref{lem:elementary-square-inequalities}). If $u \in H^s(V)$, then $u = f \in L_2(V)$ by
\Cref{lem:bessel-potential-l2}, and the first bound shows $f \in \TL{s}{2}{2}$. Conversely, for
$f \in \TL{s}{2}{2}$, $\int \langle \xi \rangle^{2s} |\widehat f|^2 < \infty$ by
\Cref{lem:tl-two-fourier}, so $f \in H^s(V)$ by \Cref{lem:bessel-potential-l2}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$H^s = \Besov{s}{2}{2}$]
\label{cor:sobolev-two-besov}
\lean{Rd.memSobolev_two_iff_exists_memApprox, Rd.memSobolev_two_iff_littlewoodPaleyNorm_lt_top,
  Rd.exists_eq_toDistr_two}
\leanok
\uses{thm:sobolev-two-triebel-lizorkin, thm:tl-diagonal, def:band-space, def:lp-blocks,
  lem:bessel-potential-l2, lem:bessel-space-enorm}
For every $s > 0$, a tempered distribution $u$ lies in $H^s(V)$ if and only if $u$ is a function
$f \in L_2(V)$ with $f \in \Besov{s}{2}{2}$, the approximation space $A^s_2$ of the
band-limited scheme. For every $s \geq 0$, $u \in H^s(V)$ if and only if $u$ is a function
$f \in L_2(V)$ with $\|f\|^{\mathrm{LP}}_{s,2} < \infty$, and every element $F$ of Mathlib's
bundled space $H^s(V)$ is a function $f \in \TL{s}{2}{2}$ with
